title: Spectrogram or wavelet of a measured signal: what frequencies are present over time?
summary: A colour map of signal power against time and frequency, above the raw trace. It shows when a tone is present, how its frequency changes and whether harmonics appear.

media.alt: A raw signal trace above a spectrogram with a rising bright ridge from about one hundred to three hundred hertz and a second ridge at twice the frequency from 1.2 seconds.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What frequencies are present over time?
read_the_figure.axes: Top: raw signal in V against time (0 to 3 s). Main panel: x time in s (shared), y frequency in Hz (0 to 800), colour power spectral density in dB (about -60 to -5). Note: sampling rate 2000 Hz, window 128 ms.
look_at: Where is the main bright ridge, and how does its frequency change?
When does a second ridge appear, and at what multiple of the first?
What is the noise level (background colour) and how far above it are the ridges?
What window length is quoted, and what does it imply for resolution?
read_the_figure.proves: A ridge that follows a smooth path in time-frequency is a tone whose frequency changes. A second ridge at twice the frequency is a harmonic. Nothing is proved about amplitude without the colour scale.
if_wrong: No window length or sampling rate: resolution cannot be judged.
Frequency axis beyond Nyquist: the picture shows aliased content.
Colour map without a dB scale: the strength of a feature is unknown.

terms.meaning: Squared magnitude of the short-time Fourier transform: power at each time and frequency.
The short segment of the signal analysed at each step; its length sets the resolution.
Power per unit frequency on a log scale: 10 log10 of the ratio to a reference.
A component at an integer multiple of a fundamental frequency.
A time-scale picture with resolution adapting to frequency, an alternative to the spectrogram.

remember: Frequency resolution = f_s / N; time resolution = N / f_s: the two trade off.
Colour in dB; state the range.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along x is time and along y is frequency; colour (viridis, dark to yellow) encodes power in dB. The top panel is the raw signal on the same time axis. The white text states the sampling rate and window; the amber arrow is an annotation naming the harmonic.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A signal whose frequency changes cannot be summarised by one spectrum. The spectrogram cuts it into short windows and shows the spectrum of each as a column of colour, so the changing content becomes a picture. The raw trace above shows that the time-frequency structure is invisible in the waveform: the ridges are buried in noise there but obvious here.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: How does the fundamental change? It rises from about 100 Hz at t = 0 to 160 Hz at t = 0.6 s, dips to 150 Hz near 1.3 s, then climbs to about 310 Hz by 2.6 s and stays there. Q2: When does the harmonic appear and where? It starts at t = 1.2 s at about 290 Hz and rises to 620 Hz at 2.6 s, which is twice the fundamental at that moment (310 x 2 = 620 Hz). Q3: What are the resolutions? The window is 128 ms at f_s = 2000 Hz (256 points): frequency resolution 7.8 Hz and time resolution 0.128 s, the product is 1 as expected.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Axes in physical units: frequency in Hz, time in seconds, power in dB. A spectrogram with pixel or bin numbers cannot be compared with anything, and is not what a measurement report needs.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The resolution trade-off blurs rapid changes if the window is long and smears frequency if it is short. The colour range hides weak features if vmin is too high and creates false structure if too low. Leakage from the window can produce ridges that are not in the signal. A dB scale compresses a factor of 100 in power to 20 dB, which makes weak harmonics look strong. Plotting beyond Nyquist is a mistake.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A scalogram (wavelet) for signals with fast transients; the Wigner distribution for sharper ridges; a plain spectrum when the signal is stationary; a ridge-tracking plot of the instantaneous frequency against time.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Overlay the instantaneous frequency estimate as a white line, mark f_N and the window length, and add a second panel with the ratio of the harmonic to the fundamental.

steps.title: Resolution of a window
steps.note: Making the window longer improves frequency resolution at the cost of time resolution.

steps.title: Nyquist limit, harmonic and dB
steps.note: The plotted range 0 to 800 Hz is inside the limit.

worked.title: Resolution and the harmonic check
worked.problem: f_s = 2000 Hz, N = 256. Find Delta f, Delta t and the Nyquist limit. At t = 2.5 s the fundamental is 310 Hz: where is the second harmonic, and by how much does a 3 dB change alter the power?
worked.answer: 7.8 Hz, 0.128 s, 1000 Hz; the harmonic is at 620 Hz (the figure shows about 620); 3 dB is a factor 2 in power.

analyze.q: The fundamental seems to rise smoothly but the true frequency may change faster than 8 Hz per window. What would you do?
What would happen at 1000 Hz and above if the signal contained those components?

evaluate.q: Is the second ridge proof of a nonlinearity in the system?
evaluate.hint: Where else can harmonics come from?

create: Draw a scalogram of the same signal and compare how it resolves the start of the harmonic.
Overlay the ridge of the fundamental and a line at twice its frequency.

checks.q: What does a ridge in the spectrogram mean?
checks.answer: A tone present at that time with that frequency.

checks.q: Window N = 512 at f_s = 2000 Hz. Frequency resolution?
A wider window sharpens the ridge in frequency but blurs the start of the harmonic. Why?
checks.answer: Delta f Delta t is fixed: a longer window averages over more time, improving frequency resolution and losing time resolution, so a sudden onset is smeared.
